paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend. An oath made before the LORD doesn't expire when the people who made it are gone (2 Samuel 21:2). Saul tried to kill the Gibeonites, and the LORD said the famine was "because of the blood shed by Saul and his family" (2 Samuel 21:1). Years had passed, and the LORD still had it on the record. I think that should make every one of us slow down before we say "I promise."

Now look at what David does. He doesn't guess why the famine came. He sought the face of the LORD first (2 Samuel 21:1). Then he sat down with the people who had been hurt and asked, "What shall I do for you?" (2 Samuel 21:3). He asked THEM, friend, and he didn't tell them what they needed. That's a whole lesson about how to deal with a wrong you had a part in. This one is heavy, and I think the pain in it is real, so I won't dress it up.

Then the story ends with something quiet. Rizpah kept her watch on a rock, and David honored the bones of Saul and Jonathan along with the seven (2 Samuel 21:10, 13). Then the passage says, "After they had done everything the king had commanded, God answered their prayers for the land" (2 Samuel 21:14). So the lesson is this: when you find out you owe somebody, seek the LORD, listen to the one who was hurt, and make it right. I've sat in a dark drawer long enough to know this, baker. It's better to deal with it than to let it sit there collecting dust.
